latin: Porcellus, simul ac loqui potuit*, ore titubante dixit<sup>1</sup>. — Tu...tu... consulto fecisti. — Casu accidit ut iterum pannum quasi loreum et saponatum in os reciperet.
Canga. — Optime carissime, mitte loqui<sup>2</sup>. — Post punctum temporis Porcellus lautus<sup>3</sup> linteo abstersus est.
... Age, sume hanc medicinam, postea cubitum ibis*.
Por. — Qu... qu..., qua de causa medicinam sumam?
Can. — Ad te corroborandum<sup>4</sup> et firmandum. Num est tibi in animo parvulum et debilem sicut Porcellum manere? Accede istuc!
Tum vero ostium pulsatum est — Veni intro! — Christophorus Robinus ingressus est.
Por. — Christophore Robine, Christophore Robine! Dic Cangae quis sim! Non desinit dicere me Ruum esse. Ego non sum Ruus, nonne?
Christophorus Robinus, eum accurate inspicit et abnuit. — Non potes Ruus esse, quia modo Ruum ludentem in domo Leporis vidi.
Can. — Heu! Mentibus fingite! Quantum me opinio fefellit<sup>5</sup>.
Chris., denuo abnuens<sup>6</sup>. — Porcellus non est. Porcellum intus et in cute novi*<sup>7</sup>: colorem diversissimum habet!
Can. — Non ignoravi eum Porcellum non esse. Aveo<sup>8</sup> scire quis sit.
Chris. — Forsitan unus ex stirpe<sup>9</sup> Pui. Filius aut patruus aut aliquis.
Porcellus se e complexu Cangae expedivit et humum desiluit<sup>10</sup>. Ingenti ejus gaudio Christophorus Robinus fores apertas reliquerat.
Nunquam tanta velocitate, quanta tunc currebat, cucurrerat, neque prius a cursu destitit quam<sup>11</sup> ad domum suam fere pervenit.
Sed cum ducentis pedibus a domo abesset*, constitit et reliquo itinere in luto<sup>12</sup> se volvit ut colorem suum jucundum et assuetum<sup>13</sup> restitueret<sup>14</sup>!
english: Piglet, as soon as he could speak, said (1) [stammering] (by a stammering mouth). — You... you've done it on purpose. — By chance it happened that he received the towel hard as leather and full of soap in his mouth once again.
Kanga. — [My cabbage] (very good), my darling, stop speaking! — [An instant] after (point of time) Piglet, washed, is dried with a towel.
... Come on, swallow this medicine, after that you'll go to bed.
P. — Wh... wh... For what reason would I take a medicine?
Kanga. — To fortify you and to [steady] you. Is it by chance [your intention] (is it to you in mind) to remain [all] small and puny like Piglet? Come here!
But at that moment [someone knocked at the door] (the door was knocked) — [Come in] (come inside)! — Christopher Robin came in.
P. — Christopher Robin, Christopher Robin! Tell Kanga who I am! She doesn't stop saying that I am Roo. I'm not Roo, am I?
Christopher Robin looks at him minutely and shakes his head. — You can't be Roo, because I [just] saw Roo playing at Rabbit's house.
Kanga. — Oh! Imagine! [How wrong I was] (how much opinion has deceived me)!
Chris., shaking his head again. — It isn't Piglet. I know Piglet inside out (see note 7): he has a completely different colour!
Kanga. — I [had noticed perfectly well] that it wasn't Piglet. I would like to know who it is.
Chris. — Perhaps [one] of Pooh's family. A son or an uncle or [someone else].
Piglet got out of Kanga's [arms] and jumped to the ground. To his great joy, Christopher Robin had left the door(s) open.
Never had he run as fast as he was running then, and he did not stop running before he had almost arrived home.
But when he was two hundred feet from his house, he stopped and [for the rest] of the way rolled in the mud so as to [restore] his pleasant and habitual colour!

footnotes: Dixit: In the previous extract, we had put the narrative in the present for you so as to simplify the reading; we leave it here in the past, as in the text by A. Lenard.

Mitto, -is, -ere, misi, missum, means first of all to let go, to let leave: Praefectus milites misit, the commander let the soldiers leave [on leave] (whence a first sense of missio, permission); here it means to renounce, to stop. But it can also mean to send off, to throw, to send someone (whence the second sense of missio, mission) or something (missile, -is, n., weapon that one throws).

Lautus (from lavo, -as, -are, lavi, lautum), to wash or to wash oneself. The form of the perfect participle is easier to understand if one remembers that u and v formerly made only one and the same letter (u, v, see preface P. X). There also exists a third form lavo, -is, -ere, lavi, lautum or lotum, which means to wash or to water, but not to wash oneself. E.g.: lavas manus, you wash your hands; but lavit mala vino, he drowns (waters) his sorrows in wine. Abstergeo, -es, -ere, tersi, tersum, to wipe (ab + tergeo, to clean).
Corroborare, to make strong, from robur, -oris, n., strength or the oak (oak).
Fallo, -is, -ere, fefelli, falsum, to deceive; falsus, -a, -um, false.

Abnuo, -is, -ere, -ui, -utum, to make a negative sign. Nutare means to make a sign of the head, to sway slightly (cf., in astronomy, nutatio, nutation, slight sway of the axis of the poles). We have already seen renuere (L. 73, N. 2).
Intus et in cute novi, w. f. w.: I know him (novi) on the inside (intus, adv.) and in the skin (cutis, L. 39, N. 10).

Aveo, -es, -ere, to desire ardently, to be avid (avidus, -a, -um). There exists a second verb avere, to be well, unrelated to the previous one, which is above all used in the imperative: Ave, Avete, Hello, Greetings. E.g.: Ave Caesar!, Hello Caesar!; Avete sodales!, Greetings mates!
Stirps, stirpis, f., stock, root of a tree, and, by extension, origin, posterity, family.

Salio, -is, -ire, salui, saltum, v.i., to jump. Derivatives: exsilire, to come out by jumping (L. 66, P. 7); insilire, to enter by jumping; desilire, to descend by jumping. Likewise sto, -as, -are, steti, statum, to stand upright, has given, through a first derivative sistere, to place, to set, the compounds: desisto, -is, -ere, destiti, v.i., to cease, to desist from, and consisto, -is, -ere, stiti, v.i., no supine, to stop, to fix oneself (cf. L. 8). You will find these two verbs P. 14 and P. 15.

Prius... quam: these two words can be separated as here, or united: priusquam. The sense remains the same, but the separation makes it possible to better highlight the function of the clauses governed by each of these elements. Ante... quam, same sense, is constructed in the same way.
Assuesco, -is, -ere, suevi, suetum, to get used to; but assuefacere (aliquem alicui rei), to accustom (s.o. to s.th.).
Restituo, -es, -ere, -ui, -utum = re + statuo (-is, -ere, statui, statutum), to put back in place, to restore.
comments: No or natare, to swim; tranare = trans + nare, to cross by swimming. — Dodrans, dodrantis, m., means on its own three quarters: est tertia hora cum dodrante, it is 3 h 3/4. We had already seen quadrans = 1/4. — To say: since how long? (question quamdudum?) one uses the ordinal numeral adjective (phrase 4: tertiam, 3rd) and the accusative. But to answer the question quamdiu? (for how long?) one uses the cardinal adjective: tres horas natavit, he swam (for) 3 hours. — Gausapa, which we saw in the previous exercise, also designates the cloth of the swimsuit and, by extension, the latter.

latin: Paule! E piscina natatoria exeas* oportet*! Quamdiu in aqua mansisti?
Aliquandiu in aqua mansi, sed non tamdiu natavi quamdiu Aemilia.
Jam pridem illa exire* debebat.
Quamdudum in piscina est? — Jamdudum! Tertiam horam in piscina est.
Horae dodrante piscinae longitudinem centies tranavit.
Cum piscina 25 m (viginti quinque metra) sit longa, duo kilometra et dimidium percurrit.
Postquam ex aqua exieris*, manutergio te abstergeto.
Corpora abstergetote! Nolite* in pulvere vos volvere dum gausapae madidae sunt.
Noli* te gerere tanquam porcellus.
Si porcelli mores imitaberis nulla crepundia accipies.
Proverbium: Nolite* projicere margaritas ante porcos.
english: Paul! You must come out of the swimming pool! How long have you been in the water?
I stayed some time in the water, but I didn't swim as long as Emily.
She ought to have come out a long time ago.
How long has she been in the pool? — [For a long time]! [For three hours] (the third hour) she has been in the pool.
In three quarters of an hour she has swum the length of the pool a hundred times.
As the pool is 25 m long, she has covered two and a half kilometres.
After you have come out of the water, dry yourself with a towel!
[Dry yourselves] (bodies)! Don't roll in the dust when [your] swimsuits are wet.
[Don't behave] (don't want to lead you) like a little pig!
If you [imitate the ways of the little pig] (will imitate), you [won't get any] toys (will receive).
Proverb: Don't throw pearls before swine = Don't give jam to pigs.
